topic: The Fundamental Bridge: The Relationship Between Integrals and Derivatives

sections.title: Intuitive Hook: The Velocity-Distance Analogy
sections.content: Introduce the concept using a squirrel gathering nuts. If we know the velocity of the squirrel, we can find its total distance (Integral). If we know its total distance over time, we can find its instantaneous velocity (Derivative). This establishes the 'inverse' relationship.
sections.example: A squirrel runs along a branch. Its velocity graph is a line; the area under this line represents the total distance traveled.

sections.title: Prerequisite Review: Rates of Change & Accumulation
sections.content: Briefly revisit the derivative as the slope of a tangent line (local change) and the integral as the area under a curve (global accumulation). Visualize these as two sides of a coin.
sections.example: Visualize a slope-field changing into a solid filled area under a curve as we 'add up' the vertical slices.

sections.title: The Fundamental Theorem: Connecting the Dots
sections.content: Formally present the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus. Show that differentiation and integration are inverse operations, effectively canceling each other out, much like multiplication and division.
sections.example: If f(x) is the rate of water flow into a tank, the integral of f(x) gives the volume, and the derivative of that volume function returns the rate of flow.

sections.title: Visual Proof: The Moving Accumulation Function
sections.content: Use an animation showing a vertical line moving across a function. As the line moves, the area to its left grows. Show that the rate at which this area grows is exactly equal to the height of the function at that point.
sections.example: An animation of a robot drawing a path: The 'Derivative' is the steering angle (instantaneous), and the 'Integral' is the resulting shape of the path traced on the floor.

sections.title: Summary & Practical Application
sections.content: Wrap up by emphasizing that integrals allow us to find 'how much' (total) while derivatives tell us 'how fast' (rate). This synergy is the foundation of modern engineering and physics.
sections.example: Engineers designing a rollercoaster: Use derivatives to ensure the track isn't too steep (safety) and integrals to ensure the train has enough energy to finish the loop.
